title: Wesley's warmed heart
hook: faith as a living trust you can feel, leading to holy love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edwards on beauty. Your line was God is beautiful. What beautiful thing got its full ten seconds? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

"In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street." That's how John Wesley begins the story in his journal. He's an Anglican priest. He has prayed, fasted, preached and served the poor, and still he doubts he has the faith he preaches. At the meeting, someone is reading aloud from Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans. And Wesley writes what happened next: "I felt my heart strangely warmed." Today: the warmed heart.

The journal goes on: "I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation." Notice what's new. Wesley already knew and preached the faith. What came that evening was trust he could feel, an assurance in the heart. For Wesley, faith isn't only agreeing that certain statements are true. It's a living trust in God that the heart can know. But the warmed heart was a beginning, not an ending. Wesley went on to preach in fields and town squares, to gather people into small groups that prayed together and kept one another honest, and to teach what he called holiness. And holiness, for Wesley, meant love: loving God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself, the commands Jesus calls the first and the second. Wesley hoped that by God's grace that love could grow until it filled a whole life. Other Christians questioned how far he pressed that hope. Methodist and other Wesleyan churches carry his teaching on. The Bible has its own warmed hearts. Two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who turns out to be the risen Jesus, and afterward they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" And the letter to the Hebrews says: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord." Wesley held those two together. The heart is warmed, and then the warmth goes to work. A feeling that never reached a neighbor, for him, would have missed the point.

Here's the practice: notice your heart. Settle, and breathe. Put a hand on your chest if you like, and feel it rise and fall. Then ask, gently: what's here right now? Warmth, coldness, tiredness, longing, nothing much? Don't fix it or judge it. Wesley wrote that he went to that meeting unwillingly; whatever you bring is enough to notice. Just notice it, as it is. If you pray, you can offer whatever you find to God, without dressing it up. The bell holds the time.
Wesley's warmed heart. Faith as a living trust you can feel, which, for Wesley, grows into holy love of God and neighbor.
Your line: heart and holiness. Today, when you feel a warm moment toward someone, turn it into one small act of love before it fades. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Methodist and other Wesleyan Christians remember Wesley's Aldersgate experience, meet in small groups for prayer and accountability, and teach growth in holy love; across churches, Christians speak of faith as heartfelt trust shown in love of neighbor.

myth: Wesley knew nothing of the Christian faith before Aldersgate
he was already a priest who preached it; what came that evening was trust he could feel.
for Wesley, holiness meant love of God and neighbor
the two commands Jesus calls first and second, growing by grace to fill a life.
someone was reading Luther when Wesley's heart was warmed
his journal: one was reading Luther's preface to the epistle to the Romans.

fork.setup: you're Wesley, the morning after your heart was strangely warmed. what comes next?
options: keep the feeling private and wait for it to come again.
go to work: preach, gather people in small groups, and grow in love.
stop praying, since the feeling is what matters.
fork.reveal: for Wesley the warm heart was a beginning. he preached, gathered small groups, and taught holiness as love of God and neighbor.

original.note: Greek, heart, the word in Luke 24:32: did not our heart burn within us?

trapdoor: what you thought: Wesley's warmed heart was just an emotional moment.
what it means: a living trust he could feel, which grew into a life of holy love.
what a scholar hears: Aldersgate, Luther on Romans read aloud, and Wesley's teaching that by grace love can fill a whole life.

notes: Wesley's journal is quoted from the original English (public domain); confirm exact wording against a standard edition, especially 'In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street' and 'I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation.' No date is given on purpose.
'He has prayed, fasted, preached and served the poor' summarizes Wesley's earlier life broadly; confirm.
Christian perfection is summarized as love growing 'until it filled a whole life'; 'other Christians questioned how far he pressed that hope' is deliberately general. Confirm fair.
Matthew 22:37–39 paraphrased; KJV says 'the first and great commandment' and 'the second is like unto it'.

Editor pass: 'already believed the right things' became 'already knew and preached the faith' (Wesley himself questioned whether he had faith before Aldersgate), with the myth item reworded to match; the practice line 'did all the right things... before he noticed his heart' rewritten to say only what the journal supports.
Audit: the practice's Wesley line was a non sequitur; replaced with one tied to the journal's 'very unwillingly'. Journal quotations match the Aldersgate entry.
